title: CNBC Interview on Fed Communications and the Case for Gradual Hikes
summary: Kashkari confirms the most hawkish position on the committee and turns it into a programme rather than a one-off objection. He dissented at the July 29 meeting in favour of +25bp (rate left at 3.50–3.75%), published an essay on July 31 calling for the Fed to begin a SERIES of small increases, and repeats that call here. The reasoning is a deliberate refusal to look through supply shocks: he concedes most of the inflation comes from successive supply shocks — the war in Iran most recently — plus an excess-demand element in AI-related categories, and argues that the source is irrelevant because 'we have one tool' and the 2% target is the Fed's job regardless of the proximate cause. He frames the hikes as calibration rather than a demand-destruction campaign ('my goal is not to slow the economy down'), which is what makes 'small' and 'series' the operative words. The secondary theme is a public jab at Warsh's communications regime: Kashkari (with Waller) defends explaining the reaction function as distinct from forward guidance, which Warsh has stripped from the statement, and is non-committal on Warsh's floated cut in the number of scheduled meetings.

key_quotes.quote: My goal is not to slow the economy down. The goal is to get inflation back down to our 2% target.
key_quotes.context: Frames the hike series as calibration to the target rather than an attempt to open slack — the reason he wants SMALL, sequential increases

key_quotes.quote: We have one tool. Now I don't think most of the inflation that we've experienced is because of economic growth and robust demand. I think most of the inflation has been because of these successive supply shocks. There is a demand element layered on top of it as well, and nonetheless, it's the Fed's job to get inflation back down to our 2% target.
key_quotes.context: His reaction function in one line: a supply-driven origin is no reason to look through, because the mandate is on the outcome not the cause

key_quotes.quote: I think there is value in continuing the tradition of explaining our reaction function to the public, and letting the public figure it out from there.
key_quotes.context: A public jab at the Warsh communications regime; he and Waller distinguish reaction-function transparency from the forward guidance Warsh has removed

key_quotes.quote: Kashkari dissented at last week's rate-setting meeting when the Fed opted to leave its policy rate unchanged in a range of 3.50% to 3.75%, saying he would have preferred a quarter-percentage-point increase.
key_quotes.context: Reuters reporting the July 29 dissent — revealed preference, not just rhetoric
